content:
The lighthouse had no name that anyone still used. Maps called it North Point, but Elias called it the throat of the weather, because every storm came in through the glass and sat in his chest until morning.

He had kept the lamp for thirty-one years. The island was a knuckle of granite, a path of salt-eaten stone, and a cottage whose roof leaked in the same three places. He patched them each autumn and pretended surprise when they opened again. The light was the only thing he refused to pretend about. If it failed, ships would find the rocks the way a hand finds a door in the dark: too late, and with too much force.

On the night the fog came in like wool packed into a wound, the radio died. Elias climbed the spiral with a can of oil and a cloth, talking to the lamp as he always did, not because he thought it listened, but because silence on a tower is a kind of falling. He trimmed the wick. He wiped the lens until the glass held a second moon.

Below, the sea moved without edges. He thought of the letters he had stopped sending, of a sister in a town with streetlamps that never had to mean anything. He thought of the boy he had been, who believed a light could be a kind of prayer.

At four, a horn answered from the fog, once, then again. Elias stood at the gallery rail and raised his lantern anyway, a smaller light beside the great one, as if to say: I am here. You are not alone in this. The horn did not come a third time. The beam turned, and turned, and kept its promise until the fog thinned to ordinary gray, and the keeper went down to make tea, counting the steps, as he had counted them all his life.
